title: Justice in the World (1971)
hookLine: bishops say acting for justice is part of preaching the gospel

lines: PART OF THE GOSPEL, OR AFTER IT?
cards: Is working for justice part of the gospel? Or is it something a Christian does afterward, on their own time, once the real religious work is done?
A synod of bishops, gathered in Rome, faced that question head on and answered in a single sentence. Not a footnote, not an appendix at the back, but near the front, where nobody could miss it.
The document goes by a plain name. Today's word is Justice in the World.

teach.b: First, the sentence. The bishops wrote that action on behalf of justice, and taking part in transforming the world, appear to them as a constitutive dimension of preaching the gospel. Constitutive is the key word.

It means part of what something is, the way flour is part of bread, not sprinkled on top. On this reading, preaching the gospel with no concern for justice would be preaching something less than the gospel.
Second, an old line behind it.

teach.h: DO JUSTICE, LOVE MERCY, WALK WITH GOD.
teach.b: The prophet Micah sums up what God asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God." Judgment there means justice, doing right by people.
It sits in the same breath as mercy and walking with God, not in a separate department. Third, a mirror. The bishops didn't only point outward.
They wrote that anyone who dares to speak to others about justice must first be just in their eyes.
So they turned to the Church's own house: how it pays the people who work for it, how it uses its property, how it treats people within its own walls. Fourth, the gap.

teach.h: GO IN PEACE, BE YE WARMED AND FILLED.
teach.b: The letter of James pictures a hungry, ill-clothed neighbor, and someone who says to them, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled", and gives them nothing. Kind words, empty hands.
Justice in the World says that gap is not small. Words of faith and acts of justice belong in the same sentence.

how: Catholic justice and peace groups, parish social-concerns committees and religious orders often cite Justice in the World as a reason their work for justice belongs at the heart of their faith, not beside it.

games.q: what does “justice in the world” mean?
o: a synod's document: justice is part of the gospel
a Vatican court that judges crimes by clergy
a UN charter that the Holy See signed in Rome

games.q: Justice in the World — tap the pairs.
p: part of what a thing is
do judgment, love mercy, walk with God

s: the bishops called justice an optional extra to the gospel
they called it a constitutive dimension of preaching the gospel.
the document asked the Church to examine its own justice
whoever speaks about justice, it says, must first be just in others' eyes.
Justice in the World was written by one pope alone
it came from a synod of bishops gathered in Rome.

games.q: you're a bishop at the synod. you're about to tell the world to be just. where do you look first?
o: at the Church's own pay, property and ways of acting.
nowhere: justice isn't the Church's business.
games.why: the bishops wrote that anyone who speaks about justice must first be just, and turned to examine the Church's own house.

practice: Look over your own day the way the bishops looked over their own house: is there someone you owe a fair share of the work, an honest answer, a bill you've been slow to pay, credit you let someone else miss?
Don't pick something heroic; find one small unfairness, real and doable, that you could put right before tonight. If you pray, ask for the courage to do it; if you don't, simply decide.

wordCard.voice: Justice in the World. The synod document saying that acting for justice is a constitutive part of preaching the gospel, beginning with the Church's own house. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: justice is gospel. Flour in the bread, not sprinkled on top. Rest well.
